L1@P0: Regular dessins with a given automorphism group
L2@P0: Gareth A. Jones
L3@P0: School of Mathematics
L4@P0: University of Southampton
L5@P0: Southampton SO17 1BJ, U.K.
L6@P0: G.A.Jones@maths.soton.ac.uk
L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: Dessins d’enfants are combinatorial structures on compact Riemann surfaces defined over
L9@P0: algebraic number fields, and regular dessins are the most symmetric of them. If G is a finite
L10@P0: group, there are only finitely many regular dessins with automorphism group G. It is shown
L11@P0: how to enumerate them, how to represent them all as quotients of a single regular dessin
L12@P0: U(G), and how certain hypermap operations act on them. For example, if G is a cyclic group
L13@P0: of order n then U(G) is a map on the Fermat curve of degree n and genus (n − 1)(n − 2)/2.
L14@P0: On the other hand, if G = A5 then U(G) has genus 274218830047232000000000000000001.
L15@P0: For other non-abelian finite simple groups, the genus is much larger.
L16@P0: MSC classification: 14H57 (primary); 14H37, 20B25, 30F10 (secondary).
L17@P0: 1 Introduction
L18@P0: Bely˘ı’s Theorem [2] states that a compact Riemann surface C, regarded as a complex projective
L19@P0: algebraic curve, can be defined over the field Q of algebraic numbers if and only if there is a
L20@P0: non-constant meromorphic function β : C → P
L21@P0: 1
L22@P0: (C) ramified over at most three points. This is
L23@P0: equivalent to the complex structure on C being obtained, in a canonical way, from a combinatorial
L24@P0: structure D on C called a dessin; this can be regarded as an oriented hypermap, a bipartite map, or
L25@P0: a tripartite triangulation of C. The most symmetric dessins are the regular dessins, those for which
L26@P0: β is a regular covering, in which case the automorphism group Aut D of D, the group of covering
L27@P0: transformations of β, and the monodromy group of β are all isomorphic to a single 2-generator
L28@P0: finite group G. In principle, understanding regular dessins is sufficient for an understanding of all
L29@P0: dessins, since each dessin arises as the quotient of some regular dessin by a group of automorphisms.
L30@P0: The set R(G) of regular dessins associated in this way with a given 2-generator finite group
L31@P0: G corresponds bijectively to the set N (G) of normal subgroups N of a free group F of rank 2 with
L32@P0: F/N ∼= G, or equivalently to the set of orbits of Aut G on generating pairs of G. Our aim here is to
L33@P0: show how a method due to Hall [20] can be used to determine the number r(G) = |R(G)| of such
L34@P0: dessins, to show how they can be represented as quotients of a single regular dessin U(G), and to
L35@P0: describe the automorphism group G = Aut U(G) of U(G). A number of illustrative examples are
L36@P0: given, including cases where G is a cyclic group, a dihedral group or a non-abelian finite simple
L37@P0: group; in the latter case, U(G) and G turn out to be surprisingly large.
L38@P0: The absolute Galois group Γ = Gal Q/Q acts on dessins by acting on the coefficients of the
L39@P0: polynomials and rational functions defining them over Q. By a recent result of Gonz´alez-Diez and
L40@P0: Jaikin-Zapirain [16], it acts faithfully on regular dessins. It preserves automorphism groups, so it
L41@P0: acts on R(G) for each G. A group Ω ∼= OutF ∼= GL2(Z) of hypermap operations, introduced by
L42@P0: James [23], also preserves regularity and automorphism groups, and its orbits on R(G) correspond
L43@P0: to the T -systems of generating pairs for G. We shall consider some examples of such actions of Γ

L1@P0: BELYI-EXTENDING MAPS AND THE GALOIS ACTION ON
L2@P0: DESSINS D’ENFANTS
L3@P0: MELANIE WOOD
L4@P0: Abstract. We study the absolute Galois group by looking for invariants and
L5@P0: orbits of its faithful action on Grothendieck’s dessins d’enfants. We define
L6@P0: a class of functions called Belyi-extending maps, which we use to construct
L7@P0: new Galois invariants of dessins from previously known invariants. Belyiextending maps are the source of the “new-type” relations on the injection
L8@P0: of the absolute Galois group into the Grothendieck-Teichm¨uller group. We
L9@P0: make explicit how to get from a general Belyi-extending map to formula for its
L10@P0: associated invariant which can be implemented in a computer algebra package.
L11@P0: We give an example of a new invariant differing on two dessins which have the
L12@P0: same values for the other readily computable invariants.
L13@P0: 1. Introduction
L14@P0: In this paper we work in the direction of a program to understand GQ =
L15@P0: Gal(Q¯ /Q), the absolute Galois group, originally sketched by Grothendieck in his
L16@P0: ambitious research outline [7]. One part of the program involves understanding GQ
L17@P0: by studying its action on certain combinatorial structures, structures so simple at
L18@P0: first glance that Grothendieck called them dessins d’enfants (children’s drawings).
L19@P0: We construct new invariants of the action of GQ on dessins d’enfants. In fact,
L20@P0: we give an example of how an invariant produced from our method distinguishes
L21@P0: between two dessin orbits on which previously known invariants agree.
L22@P0: Our basic tools are Belyi-extending maps β : P
L23@P0: 1 → P1
L24@P0: that are defined over Q,
L25@P0: ramified only over {0, 1, ∞}, and send {0, 1, ∞} into {0, 1, ∞}. These maps have
L26@P0: the property that when (X, p) is a Belyi pair, (X, β ◦ p) is also a Belyi pair. It
L27@P0: follows that each of these β acts on the set of dessins. Moreover, the action of a
L28@P0: Belyi-extending map β on dessins commutes with the GQ action on dessins. This
L29@P0: implies that two dessins Γ1 and Γ2 are in the same Galois orbit when β(Γ1) and
L30@P0: β(Γ2) are. Thus if I is a GQ-invariant of dessins (e.g. the monodromy group,
L31@P0: the rational Nielsen class), so is I ◦ β. In [5], Ellenberg defines the class of Belyiextending maps (without naming them) and notes that when I is the monodromy
L32@P0: group, the maps give new invariants as described above. He uses this perspective
L33@P0: to construct the cartographic group, but does not go any further with it.

L23: 【8†Lemma 58.2.2.】 Let $K$ be a field. Let $K^{sep}$ be a separable closure of $K$. Consider the profinite group $G = \text{Gal}(K^{sep}/K)$. The functor
L24: 
L25: \[ \begin{matrix} \text{schemes étale over }K & \longrightarrow & G\textit{-Sets} \\ X/K & \longmapsto & \mathop{\mathrm{Mor}}\nolimits _{\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(K)}(\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(K^{sep}), X) \end{matrix} \]
L26: 
L27: is an equivalence of categories.
L28: Proof. A scheme $X$ over $K$ is étale over $K$ if and only if $X \cong \coprod _{i\in I} \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(K_ i)$ with each $K_ i$ a finite separable extension of $K$ (Morphisms, Lemma 【15†29.37.7】). The functor of the lemma associates to $X$ the $G$-set
L29: 
L30: \[ \coprod \nolimits _ i \mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}\nolimits _ K(K_ i, K^{sep}) \]
L31: with its natural left $G$-action. Each element has an open stabilizer by definition of the topology on $G$. Conversely, any $G$-set $S$ is a disjoint union of its orbits. Say $S = \coprod S_ i$. Pick $s_ i \in S_ i$ and denote $G_ i \subset G$ its open stabilizer. By Galois theory (Fields, Theorem 【16†9.22.4】) the fields $(K^{sep})^{G_ i}$ are finite separable field extensions of $K$, and hence the scheme
L32: 
L33: \[ \coprod \nolimits _ i \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}((K^{sep})^{G_ i}) \]
L34: is étale over $K$. This gives an inverse to the functor of the lemma. Some details omitted. $\square$

L16: ## 58.7 Galois covers of connected schemes
L17: 
L18: Let $X$ be a connected scheme with geometric point $\overline{x}$. Since $F_{\overline{x}} : \textit{FÉt}_ X \to \textit{Sets}$ is a Galois category (Lemma 【11†58.5.5】) the material in Section 【12†58.3】 applies. In this section we explicitly transfer some of the terminology and results to the setting of schemes and finite étale morphisms.
L19: We will say a finite étale morphism $Y \to X$ is a Galois cover if $Y$ defines a Galois object of $\textit{FÉt}_ X$. For a finite étale morphism $Y \to X$ with $G = \text{Aut}_ X(Y)$ the following are equivalent
L20: 
L21:   1. $Y$ is a Galois cover of $X$,
L22: 
L23:   2. $Y$ is connected and $|G|$ is equal to the degree of $Y \to X$,
L24: 
L25:   3. $Y$ is connected and $G$ acts transitively on $F_{\overline{x}}(Y)$, and
L26: 
L27:   4. $Y$ is connected and $G$ acts simply transitively on $F_{\overline{x}}(Y)$.
L28: This follows immediately from the discussion in Section 【12†58.3】.
L29: 
L30: For any finite étale morphism $f : Y \to X$ with $Y$ connected, there is a finite étale Galois cover $Y' \to X$ which dominates $Y$ (Lemma 【13†58.3.8】).
L31: 
L32: The Galois objects of $\textit{FÉt}_ X$ correspond, via the equivalence
L33: 
L34: \[ F_{\overline{x}} : \textit{FÉt}_ X \to \textit{Finite-}\pi _1(X, \overline{x})\textit{-Sets} \]
L35: of Theorem 【14†58.6.2】, with the finite $\pi _1(X, \overline{x})\textit{-Sets}$ of the form $G = \pi _1(X, \overline{x})/H$ where $H$ is a normal open subgroup. Equivalently, if $G$ is a finite group and $\pi _1(X, \overline{x}) \to G$ is a continuous surjection, then $G$ viewed as a $\pi _1(X, \overline{x})$-set corresponds to a Galois covering.
L36: If $Y_ i \to X$, $i = 1, 2$ are finite étale Galois covers with Galois groups $G_ i$, then there exists a finite étale Galois cover $Y \to X$ whose Galois group is a subgroup of $G_1 \times G_2$. Namely, take the corresponding continuous homomorphisms $\pi _1(X, \overline{x}) \to G_ i$ and let $G$ be the image of the induced continuous homomorphism $\pi _1(X, \overline{x}) \to G_1 \times G_2$.
